newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain bids farewell as China moves into Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Britain bids farewell as China moves into Hong Kong.

text.p: Under a tropical downpour at sunset, Britain bade farewell to Hong Kong on Monday as Chinese President Jiang Zemin flew in to take back the colony and People's Liberation Army troops crossed the border.

A cavalcade of open-backed trucks and buses carrying 509 lightly-armed Chinese troops -- ordered to "love the people of Hong Kong" -- moved in during an end-of-empire extravaganza at Victoria Harbour.

They drove quickly to the Prince of Wales barracks in the city centre, across a harbourside street from the British royal yacht Britannia, preparing to take heir to the throne Prince Charles home after he hands back the territory.
A second and major wave of 4,000 troops backed by armour, helicopters and warships was set to sweep in at dawn on Tuesday.

Bagpipers, dragon dancers and massed choirs entertained a crowd of 10,000 huddling under umbrellas at the farewell bash attended by Prince Charles, outgoing governor Chris Patten and a host of world dignitaries.

More than 100 million television viewers around the world witnessed the pomp and pageantry of Britain's retreat from the last major outpost of Empire, a "barren rock" that became a glittering capitalist trading city.
A dazzling fireworks display lit up the harbour, illuminating the Britannia and the missile batteries of its escort frigate HMS Chatham.

At a sumptuous banquet at the Hong Kong convention centre Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen proposed a toast to Jiang, Britain's Queen Elizabeth and the "long term stability and prosperity of Hong Kong".

In the final hours of British rule, Britain and China began patching up a row over democratic reforms introduced by Hong Kong's 28th and last governor who Beijing had condemned as a "whore", a "sinner" and a "villain".

Jiang, the only Chinese head of state to set foot in Hong Kong, met British Prime Minister Tony Blair for the first time and invited him to China. Blair urged Jiang to forget past battles and build a new relationship.
The Chinese president flew in with Premier Li Peng and Zhuo Lin, widow of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, who had died four months before he could fulfil a lifelong wish to see the reunification.

Schoolchildren waving plastic flowers and red five-star flags of China cheered as he was greeted by incoming Hong Kong chief executive Tung Chee-hwa, 60, a shipping magnate chosen by Beijing to run the city of 6.4 million people.
At the stroke of midnight (1600 GMT), Jiang was to receive the Crown Colony back from Prince Charles, ending an imperial reign of 156 years.

In Beijing, Tiananmen Square was a blaze of neon light and colour as dancers and folk singers on a vast stage entertained a crowd of 100,000 celebrating an event that banners proclaimed would "wash away 100 years of shame".
For China, the return of Hong Kong to the motherland and the departure of the last colonists from its shores erases an era of humiliation dating from 19th century Opium Wars with Britain.
But the swift dispatch of troops has angered Hong Kong democrats, who still have nightmares over the PLA's crushing of democratic dissent around Tiananmen in 1989.
Half an hour before Jiang's Air China flight touched down, Patten was swept from Government House in a black Rolls Royce to the strains of "Auld Lang Syne".

Patten, 53, choked back tears, and his wife and three daughters were misty-eyed, as a police bugler played the Last Post on the lawns of the colonial mansion and the Union Jack was lowered and wrapped up for him to take away.

Wearing a ceremonial sword at the harbour festivities, Prince Charles read a message from his mother Queen Elizabeth, in which she stressed Hong Kong's future depended on faithful implementation by Beijing of a 1984 Sino-British agreement.

Under the accord, Beijing promised that Hong Kong would enjoy autonomy under a unique "one country, two systems" formula under which rampantly capitalist Hong Kong would retain its freedoms for 50 years.

Patten, rain soaking his suit, fought tears after an ovation for his farewell speech when he declared that Hong Kong's "unshakeable destiny" was to run its own affairs. No dependent territory had ever achieved more prosperity, he said.
Tung, a billionaire whose Chinese name means "build China", has promised popular elections for a new legislature next May.

The democratically-elected Legislative Council was to be replaced by a Beijing-picked Provisional Legislature soon after midnight, putting several of the territory's most popular politicians out of a job.
Veteran democrat Martin Lee told reporters freedom was what had made Hong Kong the Pearl of the Orient.
"The lustre of the pearl is our freedom. If we lose our freedom, that pearl loses its lustre," he said.
